paper.title: The Unequal Consequences of Job Loss across Countries
paper.code_data_availability: Replication package: Bertheau, Antoine, Edoardo Maria Acabbi, Cristina Barceló, Andreas Gulyas, Stefano Lombardi, and Raffaele Saggio. …

registers.name_in_paper: matched employer-employee administrative register, Denmark (data access from Denmark Statistics; sources listed in online Appendix Table A.10)
matched employer-employee administrative register, Sweden (data access from IFAU Uppsala)
matched employer-employee administrative register, France (random sample of individuals with all their employment spells; data access from the CASD)
LOSAI (Italian matched employer-employee data provided by the Segretariato Ufficio Statistica at the Italian Ministry of Labour; random sample of individuals)
matched employer-employee administrative register, Spain (random sample of individuals with all their employment spells)
registers.years: years of job loss 2007–2019; data on job displacements available from 2007 onward

linkages: Workers are linked to establishments in each country's matched employer-employee register; the main employer is the establishment at which the worker's annual earnings are largest, and the unit of analysis for the employer is the establishment.

Each displaced worker is linked 1:1, without replacement, to a nearest-neighbour propensity-score-matched control worker within cells defined by calendar year, gender and industry of the displaced worker.
Employer-specific wage premiums are linked to workers through the establishment identifier J(i,t) used in the AKM model, equation (2).

sample.universe: Workers covered by harmonized matched employer-employee administrative registers in Austria, Denmark, France, Italy, Portugal, Spain and Sweden; for France, Italy and Spain the data are a random sample of individuals with all their employment spells rather than the universe.
sample.unit_of_observation: person-year (worker i in calendar year t)
selection_rules: Workers at most 50 years old in the year preceding the job displacement event (to limit the influence of early retirement programs).
Workers with at least three years of tenure with their main employer in the year preceding the job displacement event (stable jobs).
Workers employed in establishments with at least 50 employees at the end of the predisplacement year.
Treated: workers who (i) separate from their main employer in t* and (ii) whose current establishment's employment drops by at least 30 percent in t*.
Workers recalled by their main employer within five years of displacement are dropped from both the treatment and the control group.
Displacement events in which more than 20 percent of workers jointly move to another firm are excluded (to avoid classifying mergers or domestic outsourcing as mass layoffs).
Potential control workers are those who do not concurrently satisfy both treatment conditions; identical sampling restrictions are applied to control workers.
1:1 nearest neighbour propensity-score matching without replacement within cells defined by calendar year, gender and industry of the displaced worker.
Wage outcomes are computed only for the subset of employed person-years.

For Table 3, the wage regressions use the subsample of person-years whose employer at time t belongs to the within-country largest connected set of firms associated with equation (2); treated and control workers are excluded when equation (2) is estimated.
Workers are followed from five years before to five years after the job displacement event.
sample.period: Job loss events due to mass layoffs occurring between at least the 1990s and the 2010s. Years of job loss by country (Table 1): Denmark 1983–2017, Sweden 1994–2016, Italy 1993–2016, Spain 2007–2019, Austria 1987–2018, France 1994–2016, Portugal 1992–2017.
sample.n_observations: Person-year observations in thousands (Table 2, earnings column): Denmark 4,295; Sweden 2,247; Austria 1,192; France 577; Italy 1,526; Spain 302; Portugal 3,491. Wage column: Denmark 3,701; Sweden 2,169; Austria 1,119; France 542; Italy 1,304; Spain 277; Portugal 2,692. Table 3: Denmark 3,674; Sweden 1,937; Austria 1,048; France 489; Italy 1,262; Spain 259; Portugal 2,525.
sample.n_individuals: Number of workers in thousands, treated and control separately (Table 1): Denmark 201.91; Sweden 108.58; Italy 66.07; Spain 14.71; Austria 55.82; France 28.64; Portugal 171.14.

construction_notes: Earnings are deflated to 2010 EUR and defined as the sum of yearly labor earnings (possibly from different employers) before taxation; they include overtime, bonuses and severance payments when available.
Wages are defined as daily earnings from the main employer, computed as labor earnings over days worked; information on hours worked is not available for all countries.
A person is defined as employed if they have any positive labor earnings during the year; zero earnings are imputed for years of nonemployment.
The main employer is the establishment at which the worker's annual earnings are largest; the unit of analysis for the employer is the establishment.

The propensity score is estimated by probit within cells of calendar year, gender and industry; it includes earnings in t*−2 and t*−3, age, tenure and employer size in t*−1, plus contract type (temporary versus permanent) and full-time status in t*−1 where available.
Explicit information on the reason for job separation (layoff versus voluntary resignation) is available and used for Spain and Italy.
The event study coefficients {θ_k} are normalized relative to θ_{−3}; X_it includes age squared; standard errors are clustered at the worker level.
In Table 2, the point estimates on earnings are rescaled by the average earnings measured in the predisplacement years, and the coefficients on earnings and employment are multiplied by 100.

The AKM model, equation (2), is estimated separately for each country on workers with positive earnings, with worker and establishment fixed effects, year indicators and a cubic polynomial in age, excluding the treated and control workers.

Column 3 of Table 3 is the ratio of the job displacement effect on the employer-specific wage premium (column 1) to the overall job displacement effect on log wages (column 2), following Lachowska, Mas, and Woodbury (2020).
Figure 2 uses the cohort of workers displaced in the year 2010, to maximize comparability across countries.
Industry groups were matched at a more disaggregated country-specific level but are reaggregated in Table 1 for presentation purposes.

claims.statement: Job displacement through a mass layoff reduces the total yearly labor earnings of displaced workers in Denmark by 17.85 percent of their average predisplacement earnings 1 year after the event, relative to matched non-displaced workers.

treatment.label: Job displacement through a mass layoff (Displaced_i × event time k)

definition.value: Displaced_i is an indicator equal to one for treated workers who lose their job in a displacement event. A displacement event in year t* requires that (i) the worker separates from their main employer in t* and (ii) employment at the current establishment drops by at least 30 percent in t*. The sample is restricted to workers at most 50 years old in t*−1, with at least three years of tenure with their main employer in t*−1, employed in an establishment with at least 50 employees at the end of t*−1. Workers recalled by their main employer within five years, and events in which more than 20 percent of workers jointly move to another firm, are excluded.

timing.value: Year of the displacement event, t*; the treatment indicator is interacted with event time k = −5, ..., 5 relative to t*

definition.value: Earnings, deflated to 2010 EUR, defined as the sum of yearly labor earnings (possibly from different employers) before taxation; labor earnings include overtime, bonuses and severance payments when available. Zero earnings are imputed for years in which the person is nonemployed. In Table 2 the point estimates are rescaled by the average earnings measured in the predisplacement years and multiplied by 100.

timing.value: Measured in calendar year t; the reported coefficient is for event time k = 1, i.e. 1 year after the displacement year t*

units.value: percent of average predisplacement earnings (coefficient rescaled by average predisplacement earnings and multiplied by 100)

magnitude.interpretation: One year after displacement, postdisplacement earnings are 20 percent lower compared to earnings measured in the predisplacement years; this effect is twice as large in southern Europe.

estimand.target_population: Workers in Denmark who are displaced through a mass layoff and who satisfy the sample restrictions (at most 50 years old, at least three years of tenure, establishment with at least 50 employees in t*−1)
estimand.time_horizon: event time k = 1, i.e. 1 year after the displacement event

population.description: Workers in Denmark displaced through a mass layoff — at most 50 years old, with at least three years of tenure with their main employer and employed in an establishment with at least 50 employees in the year before displacement — and their 1:1 propensity-score-matched non-displaced control workers
population.ages: at most 50 years old in the year preceding the job displacement event
population.period: years of job loss 1983–2017 (Table 1, panel A)
subgroups_defined: displaced (treated) versus matched control workers
men and women (online Appendix Figure A.2; online Appendix Table A.8)

population.selection: Displaced workers are matched 1:1, without replacement, to nearest-neighbour control workers on a propensity score estimated by probit within cells defined by calendar year, gender, and industry; the score uses earnings in t*−2 and t*−3, age, tenure and employer size in t*−1, plus contract type and full-time status where available. Workers recalled by their main employer within five years of displacement are dropped from both groups, and displacement events in which more than 20 percent of workers jointly move to another firm are excluded. Identical sampling restrictions are applied to control workers.

identification.source_of_variation: Job displacement through a mass layoff: separation from the main employer in t* combined with a drop of at least 30 percent in establishment employment in t*, in establishments with at least 50 employees; displaced workers are compared with 1:1 propensity-score-matched workers who do not experience such an event.

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends between displaced (treated) and matched control workers: absent displacement, the two groups' outcomes would have evolved in the same way relative to event time k = −3.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated at equation (1) as the condition under which θ_k capture the causal effect of job loss; supported by the pre-event coefficients for k = −5 ... −1 plotted in Figure 1 and by the balance of observable characteristics between treated and matched control workers in Table 1.

formal.as_written: Under the assumption of parallel trends between the treated and control units, the coefficients of interest, θ_k, capture the causal effect of job loss at event time k.

key_assumptions.assumption: The separations studied are exogenous and permanent: a drop of at least 30 percent in establishment employment in t* identifies involuntary mass-layoff separations rather than voluntary quits.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The 30 percent threshold is described as standard in the mass layoff literature; explicit information on the reason for job separation (layoff versus voluntary resignation) is used for Spain and Italy, and online Appendix Figure A.4 shows the results are unaffected when it is not used.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the matching variables (calendar year, gender, industry, earnings in t*−2 and t*−3, age, tenure, employer size in t*−1, and where available contract type and full-time status), matched control workers are a valid comparison group — the estimation sample is conditioned on the propensity-score match.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 1 shows treated and matched comparison workers with well-balanced observable characteristics in every country.

threats_discussed: Existing cross-country comparisons are clouded by differences in sample selection, the definition of the displacement event, the control group and the time period (Section I).
Mischaracterising voluntary separations as layoffs (addressed by the 30 percent employment-drop restriction and, for Spain and Italy, by explicit separation-reason information).
Mass layoffs select only a subset of involuntary separations (footnote 4).
Mergers and domestic outsourcing events could be classified as mass layoffs (footnote 3; events in which more than 20 percent of workers jointly move to another firm are excluded).
For France, Italy and Spain the data are a random sample of individuals rather than the universe of administrative records (footnote 6).
Quadros de Pessoal provides only an October snapshot, so Portuguese displaced workers are by construction nonemployed or at a different employer in t* (footnote 7).
Cross-country differences in observed characteristics (online Appendix B).
Differences across countries in the coverage of self-employment or public jobs (online Appendix D).
robustness_checks: Online Appendix Table A.2: imposing the tenure restriction on control workers can double the estimated earnings losses.
Online Appendix Figure A.4: results are unaffected when the reason for job separation is not used for Spain and Italy.

Online Appendix Figure A.2: job loss effects estimated separately for men and women.
Online Appendix Table A.6: comparison with Germany using the estimates of Schmieder, von Wachter, and Heining (2023).
Shifting the event time for Portugal by one year (footnote 7).
Online Appendix B: cross-country differences in observed characteristics.
Online Appendix D: coverage of self-employment and public jobs.
unresolved_confounders: Mass layoffs select only a subset of involuntary separations, which the authors note as a drawback of the design (footnote 4).

heterogeneity.finding: Five years after displacement, northern European workers still suffer a 10 percent loss in total earnings compared to a 30 percent loss for their southern European counterparts; Austrian workers face earnings losses somewhere in between, while French workers have earnings losses more similar to what was observed in the Scandinavian countries.
When estimating the effects of job displacement separately by men and women, the remarkable differences in earnings losses across countries remain unaltered (online Appendix Figure A.2).

Italy is the only country with a remarkable time trend in the job loss effects: Italian workers suffered earnings losses of around 25 percent in the 1990s but of 40 percent in the 2010s (online Appendix Figure A.1).

ambiguities: The paper prints standard errors but no significance stars, confidence intervals or p-values; statistically_significant is inferred from the ratio of the printed estimate to its printed standard error (see the derivation evidence record).

Table 2's earnings coefficients are rescaled by average predisplacement earnings, so no baseline mean is printed in the coefficient's own units; the baseline_mean recorded is the control group's mean earnings in t*−3 from Table 1, in thousands of 2010 EUR.

evidence.annotation: Notes: The figure shows event study estimates of the job loss effects from equation (1). Estimates are relative to t* − 3, where t* is the job loss year. The coefficients in panel A are rescaled using average predisplacement labor earnings. The outcome in panel B is an indicator equal to one if a worker has at least one day of work in the corresponding year. Point estimates and standard errors are displayed in Table 2.

evidence.how: Statistical significance is not marked in the paper. It is inferred here from the ratio of the printed point estimate (-17.85) to its printed standard error (0.155), which is 115 in absolute value.

Table 2's earnings coefficients are rescaled by average predisplacement earnings, so no baseline mean is printed in the coefficient's own scale. The baseline recorded here is the control group's mean earnings in t*−3 for Denmark printed in Table 1 (40.2 thousand 2010 EUR); the treated-group mean is 40.3. The recorded outcome_sd is the matching standard deviation printed in parentheses for the control group (23.5).

value.as_printed: y_it = α_i + λ_t + ∑_{k=−5}^{k=5} γ_k 1{t = t*_i + k} + ∑_{k=−5}^{k=5} θ_k 1{t = t*_i + k} × Displaced_i + X'_it β + r_it
value.lhs: y_it, the dependent variable: total yearly earnings, employment status, or log daily wages in year t (in Table 3, column 1, the estimated AKM employer wage premium)
value.normalisation: The coefficients {θ_k} are normalized relative to θ_{−3}, i.e. to event year k = −3. The point estimates on earnings are rescaled by the average earnings measured in the predisplacement years, and the coefficients on earnings and employment are multiplied by 100.

theory_referenced: More efficient labor markets reallocate workers more quickly and generate lower earnings losses after job displacement — earnings losses as a proxy for how well labor markets are functioning

prior_findings_compared.citation: Leombruni, Razzolini, and Serti (2013); Bennett and Ouazad (2020)
prior_findings_compared.as_stated: Interestingly, existing evidence leads to drastically different conclusions from ours.

outcomes_examined_not_reported: Additional analyses on the potential role of institutions are reported in the working paper version of this article (Bertheau et al. 2022), not in this paper.

definition.value: Displaced_i is an indicator equal to one for treated workers who lose their job in a displacement event. claims.statement: Job displacement through a mass layoff reduces the probability that displaced workers in Austria are employed by 17.42 percentage points 1 year after the event, relative to matched non-displaced workers.

definition.value: Displaced_i is an indicator equal to one for treated workers who lose their job in a displacement event. definition.value: Displaced_i is an indicator equal to one for treated workers who lose their job in a displacement event. A displacement event in year t* requires that (i) the worker separates from their main employer in t* and (ii) employment at the current establishment drops by at least 30 percent in t*. The sample is restricted to workers at most 50 years old in t*−1, with at least three years of tenure with their main employer in t*−1, employed in an establishment with at least 50 employees at the end of t*−1. Workers recalled by their main employer within five years, and events in which more than 20 percent of workers jointly move to another firm, are excluded.

Workers recalled by their main employer within five years of displacement are dropped from both groups, and displacement events in which more than 20 percent of workers jointly move to another firm are excluded. definition.value: Displaced_i is an indicator equal to one for treated workers who lose their job in a displacement event. claims.statement: Among workers who are employed, job displacement through a mass layoff reduces the log daily wage of displaced workers in Spain by 0.17 log points 5 years after the event, relative to matched non-displaced workers.

treatment.label: Job displacement through a mass layoff (Displaced_i × event time k)

definition.value: Displaced_i is an indicator equal to one for treated workers who lose their job in a displacement event. A displacement event in year t* requires that (i) the worker separates from their main employer in t* and (ii) employment at the current establishment drops by at least 30 percent in t*. The sample is restricted to workers at most 50 years old in t*−1, with at least three years of tenure with their main employer in t*−1, employed in an establishment with at least 50 employees at the end of t*−1. Workers recalled by their main employer within five years, and events in which more than 20 percent of workers jointly move to another firm, are excluded.

timing.value: Year of the displacement event, t*; the treatment indicator is interacted with event time k = −5, ..., 5 relative to t*

definition.value: Wages are defined as daily earnings from the main employer and are computed as labor earnings over days worked; the outcome is the log of the daily wage. Wages are computed only for the subset of employed workers, so the wage sample is smaller than the earnings sample. Hours worked are not available for all countries.

timing.value: Measured in calendar year t; the reported coefficient is for event time k = 5, i.e. 5 years after the displacement year t*

units.value: log points of the daily wage

magnitude.interpretation: Losses in daily wages range from about 4 percent (Denmark) to 17 percent (Spain) five years after displacement.

population.selection: Displaced workers are matched 1:1, without replacement, to nearest-neighbour control workers on a propensity score estimated by probit within cells defined by calendar year, gender, and industry; the score uses earnings in t*−2 and t*−3, age, tenure and employer size in t*−1, plus contract type and full-time status where available. Workers recalled by their main employer within five years of displacement are dropped from both groups, and displacement events in which more than 20 percent of workers jointly move to another firm are excluded. Identical sampling restrictions are applied to control workers. For Spain the data are not the universe of administrative records but a random sample of individuals with all their employment spells (4% of the universe). Wages are computed only for the subset of employed workers, so the wage sample is restricted to employed person-years.

definition.value: Displaced_i is an indicator equal to one for treated workers who lose their job in a displacement event. definition.value: Displaced_i is an indicator equal to one for treated workers who lose their job in a displacement event. claims.statement: Job displacement through a mass layoff reduces the employer-specific (AKM) wage premium of displaced workers in Sweden by 0.027 log points 1 year after the event, relative to matched non-displaced workers.

treatment.label: Job displacement through a mass layoff (Displaced_i × event time k)

definition.value: Displaced_i is an indicator equal to one for treated workers who lose their job in a displacement event. A displacement event in year t* requires that (i) the worker separates from their main employer in t* and (ii) employment at the current establishment drops by at least 30 percent in t*. The sample is restricted to workers at most 50 years old in t*−1, with at least three years of tenure with their main employer in t*−1, employed in an establishment with at least 50 employees at the end of t*−1. Workers recalled by their main employer within five years, and events in which more than 20 percent of workers jointly move to another firm, are excluded.

timing.value: Year of the displacement event, t*; the treatment indicator is interacted with event time k = −5, ..., 5 relative to t*

definition.value: The estimated establishment fixed effect ψ̂_{J(i,t)} from the Abowd-Kramarz-Margolis model, equation (2), for log daily wage, where J(i,t) is the main employer of worker i in year t. The AKM model is estimated for each country on the sample of workers with positive earnings, excluding the treated and control workers, with worker and establishment fixed effects, year indicators and a cubic polynomial in age. ψ_{J(i,t)} captures the time-invariant wage policy component for a given employer, denoted the employer-specific wage premium.

timing.value: Measured in calendar year t; the reported coefficient is for event time k = 1, i.e. 1 year after the displacement year t*

units.value: log points of the AKM employer-specific wage premium

magnitude.interpretation: The loss of employer-specific wage premiums is very important in explaining overall wage losses across all countries.

estimand.target_population: Workers in Sweden who are displaced through a mass layoff, satisfy the sample restrictions, are employed, and whose employer belongs to the within-country largest connected set of firms associated with equation (2)
estimand.time_horizon: event time k = 1, i.e. 1 year after the displacement event

population.description: Workers in Sweden displaced through a mass layoff — at most 50 years old, with at least three years of tenure with their main employer and employed in an establishment with at least 50 employees in the year before displacement — and their 1:1 propensity-score-matched non-displaced control workers
population.ages: at most 50 years old in the year preceding the job displacement event
population.period: years of job loss 1994–2016 (Table 1, panel A)
subgroups_defined: displaced (treated) versus matched control workers
men and women (online Appendix Figure A.2; online Appendix Table A.8)
decade of displacement (online Appendix Figure A.1)
population.selection: Displaced workers are matched 1:1, without replacement, to nearest-neighbour control workers on a propensity score estimated by probit within cells defined by calendar year, gender, and industry; the score uses earnings in t*−2 and t*−3, age, tenure and employer size in t*−1, plus contract type and full-time status where available. Workers recalled by their main employer within five years of displacement are dropped from both groups, and displacement events in which more than 20 percent of workers jointly move to another firm are excluded. Identical sampling restrictions are applied to control workers. Wages are computed only for the subset of employed workers, and the Table 3 estimates use the subsample of displaced and matched control workers whose employer at time t belongs to the within-country largest connected set of firms associated with equation (2). The AKM model, equation (2), is estimated on the country's workers with positive earnings, excluding the treated and control workers.

population.selection: Displaced workers are matched 1:1, without replacement, to nearest-neighbour control workers on a propensity score estimated by probit within cells defined by calendar year, gender, and industry; the score uses earnings in t*−2 and t*−3, age, tenure and employer size in t*−1, plus contract type and full-time status where available. claims.statement: Job displacement through a mass layoff reduces the employer-specific (AKM) wage premium of displaced workers in Austria by 0.061 log points 1 year after the event, relative to matched non-displaced workers.

treatment.label: Job displacement through a mass layoff (Displaced_i × event time k)

definition.value: Displaced_i is an indicator equal to one for treated workers who lose their job in a displacement event. A displacement event in year t* requires that (i) the worker separates from their main employer in t* and (ii) employment at the current establishment drops by at least 30 percent in t*. The sample is restricted to workers at most 50 years old in t*−1, with at least three years of tenure with their main employer in t*−1, employed in an establishment with at least 50 employees at the end of t*−1. Workers recalled by their main employer within five years, and events in which more than 20 percent of workers jointly move to another firm, are excluded.

timing.value: Year of the displacement event, t*; the treatment indicator is interacted with event time k = −5, ..., 5 relative to t*

definition.value: The estimated establishment fixed effect ψ̂_{J(i,t)} from the Abowd-Kramarz-Margolis model, equation (2), for log daily wage, where J(i,t) is the main employer of worker i in year t. The AKM model is estimated for each country on the sample of workers with positive earnings, excluding the treated and control workers, with worker and establishment fixed effects, year indicators and a cubic polynomial in age. ψ_{J(i,t)} captures the time-invariant wage policy component for a given employer, denoted the employer-specific wage premium.

timing.value: Measured in calendar year t; the reported coefficient is for event time k = 1, i.e. 1 year after the displacement year t*

units.value: log points of the AKM employer-specific wage premium

magnitude.interpretation: The loss of employer-specific wage premiums is very important in explaining overall wage losses across all countries.

definition.value: Displaced_i is an indicator equal to one for treated workers who lose their job in a displacement event. A displacement event in year t* requires that (i) the worker separates from their main employer in t* and (ii) employment at the current establishment drops by at least 30 percent in t*. The sample is restricted to workers at most 50 years old in t*−1, with at least three years of tenure with their main employer in t*−1, employed in an establishment with at least 50 employees at the end of t*−1. Workers recalled by their main employer within five years, and events in which more than 20 percent of workers jointly move to another firm, are excluded.

timing.value: Year of the displacement event, t*; the treatment indicator is interacted with event time k = −5, ..., 5 relative to t*

definition.value: The log of the daily wage, i.e. labor earnings from the main employer over days worked, estimated on the subsample of displaced and matched control workers whose employer at time t belongs to the within-country largest connected set of firms associated with equation (2).

timing.value: Measured in calendar year t; the reported coefficient is for event time k = 5, i.e. 5 years after the displacement year t*

units.value: log points of the daily wage

estimand.target_population: Workers in Austria who are displaced through a mass layoff, satisfy the sample restrictions, are employed, and whose employer belongs to the within-country largest connected set of firms associated with equation (2)
estimand.time_horizon: event time k = 5, i.e. 5 years after the displacement event

population.description: Workers in Austria displaced through a mass layoff — at most 50 years old, with at least three years of tenure with their main employer and employed in an establishment with at least 50 employees in the year before displacement — and their 1:1 propensity-score-matched non-displaced control workers
population.ages: at most 50 years old in the year preceding the job displacement event
population.period: years of job loss 1987–2018 (Table 1, panel A)
subgroups_defined: displaced (treated) versus matched control workers
men and women (online Appendix Figure A.2; online Appendix Table A.8)
decade of displacement (online Appendix Figure A.1)
population.selection: Displaced workers are matched 1:1, without replacement, to nearest-neighbour control workers on a propensity score estimated by probit within cells defined by calendar year, gender, and industry; the score uses earnings in t*−2 and t*−3, age, tenure and employer size in t*−1, plus contract type and full-time status where available. Workers recalled by their main employer within five years of displacement are dropped from both groups, and displacement events in which more than 20 percent of workers jointly move to another firm are excluded. Identical sampling restrictions are applied to control workers. Wages are computed only for the subset of employed workers, and the Table 3 estimates use the subsample of displaced and matched control workers whose employer at time t belongs to the within-country largest connected set of firms associated with equation (2). The AKM model, equation (2), is estimated on the country's workers with positive earnings, excluding the treated and control workers.

identification.source_of_variation: Job displacement through a mass layoff: separation from the main employer in t* combined with a drop of at least 30 percent in establishment employment in t*; displaced workers are compared with 1:1 propensity-score-matched workers who do not experience such an event. For column 1 the dependent variable is the employer wage premium estimated in a separate AKM first step.

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends between displaced (treated) and matched control workers: absent displacement, the two groups' outcomes would have evolved in the same way relative to event time k = −3.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated at equation (1) as the condition under which θ_k capture the causal effect of job loss; supported by the pre-event coefficients for k = −5 ... −1 plotted in Figure 1 and by the balance of observable characteristics between treated and matched control workers in Table 1.

formal.as_written: Under the assumption of parallel trends between the treated and control units, the coefficients of interest, θ_k, capture the causal effect of job loss at event time k.

key_assumptions.assumption: The separations studied are exogenous and permanent: a drop of at least 30 percent in establishment employment in t* identifies involuntary mass-layoff separations rather than voluntary quits.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The 30 percent threshold is described as standard in the mass layoff literature; explicit information on the reason for job separation (layoff versus voluntary resignation) is used for Spain and Italy, and online Appendix Figure A.4 shows the results are unaffected when it is not used.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the matching variables (calendar year, gender, industry, earnings in t*−2 and t*−3, age, tenure, employer size in t*−1, and where available contract type and full-time status), matched control workers are a valid comparison group — the estimation sample is conditioned on the propensity-score match.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 1 shows treated and matched comparison workers with well-balanced observable characteristics in every country.

implies_edges.from: pre-displacement characteristics used in the propensity score
implies_edges.to: analysis sample (1:1 matched displaced and control workers)

key_assumptions.assumption: The analysis sample is conditioned on the separation being permanent: workers recalled by their main employer within five years of displacement, and events in which more than 20 percent of workers jointly move to another firm, are dropped from both the treatment and the control group.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a sample-construction rule in footnote 3; no separate test is reported.

implies_edges.from: recall by the main employer within five years of displacement
implies_edges.to: analysis sample (1:1 matched displaced and control workers)

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation of the displacement event at the normalisation period: the coefficients {θ_k} are normalized relative to θ_{−3}, which treats event year k = −3 as unaffected by the later job loss.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states the normalisation and plots pre-event coefficients from k = −5, but does not state or test a no-anticipation condition.

implies_edges.from: job displacement through a mass layoff
implies_edges.to: outcome at event time k = −3

key_assumptions.assumption: Wages are observed only for employed person-years, so the wage sample is conditioned on post-displacement employment (selection on reemployment).
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states wages are computed only for the subset of employed workers and reports Lee (2009) bounds accounting for selection on reemployment in online Appendix Table A.9.

implies_edges.from: being employed after displacement
implies_edges.to: analysis sample (1:1 matched displaced and control workers)

key_assumptions.assumption: Log daily wages are additively separable into a worker effect, a time-invariant establishment wage-policy effect ψ_{J(i,t)} and a year effect (AKM, equation (2)), so that ψ̂_{J(i,t)} measures the employer-specific wage premium.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Equation (2) is printed; the paper cites Abowd, Kramarz, and Margolis (1999) and Card, Cardoso, and Kline (2016) for the interpretation. No specification test of the AKM form is reported in this paper.

formal.as_written: y_it = α_i + ψ_{J(i,t)} + λ_t + X'_it β + u_it

key_assumptions.assumption: Job loss itself does not contribute to the estimated establishment effects: treated and control workers are excluded when equation (2) is estimated.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a construction choice; no separate test is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: The wage regressions of Table 3 are restricted to person-years whose employer belongs to the within-country largest connected set of firms associated with equation (2).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in footnote 12 and in the note to Table 3.

implies_edges.from: employer belongs to the within-country largest connected set of firms
implies_edges.to: analysis sample (1:1 matched displaced and control workers)

threats_discussed: Existing cross-country comparisons are clouded by differences in sample selection, the definition of the displacement event, the control group and the time period (Section I).
Mischaracterising voluntary separations as layoffs (addressed by the 30 percent employment-drop restriction and, for Spain and Italy, by explicit separation-reason information).
Mass layoffs select only a subset of involuntary separations (footnote 4).
Mergers and domestic outsourcing events could be classified as mass layoffs (footnote 3; events in which more than 20 percent of workers jointly move to another firm are excluded).
For France, Italy and Spain the data are a random sample of individuals rather than the universe of administrative records (footnote 6).
Quadros de Pessoal provides only an October snapshot, so Portuguese displaced workers are by construction nonemployed or at a different employer in t* (footnote 7).
Cross-country differences in observed characteristics (online Appendix B).
Differences across countries in the coverage of self-employment or public jobs (online Appendix D).
Wages are computed only for the subset of employed workers, so wage effects are conditioned on reemployment (online Appendix Table A.9 reports Lee (2009) bounds).

claims.statement: Job displacement through a mass layoff reduces the employer-specific (AKM) wage premium of displaced workers in France by 0.025 log points 1 year after the event, relative to matched non-displaced workers.

treatment.label: Job displacement through a mass layoff (Displaced_i × event time k)

definition.value: Displaced_i is an indicator equal to one for treated workers who lose their job in a displacement event. A displacement event in year t* requires that (i) the worker separates from their main employer in t* and (ii) employment at the current establishment drops by at least 30 percent in t*. timing.value: Year of the displacement event, t*; the treatment indicator is interacted with event time k = −5, ..., 5 relative to t*

definition.value: The estimated establishment fixed effect ψ̂_{J(i,t)} from the Abowd-Kramarz-Margolis model, equation (2), for log daily wage, where J(i,t) is the main employer of worker i in year t. timing.value: Measured in calendar year t; the reported coefficient is for event time k = 1, i.e. 1 year after the displacement year t*

units.value: log points of the AKM employer-specific wage premium

magnitude.interpretation: The loss of employer-specific wage premiums is very important in explaining overall wage losses across all countries.

claims.statement: Job displacement through a mass layoff reduces the employer-specific (AKM) wage premium of displaced workers in France by 0.03 log points 5 years after the event, relative to matched non-displaced workers.

treatment.label: Job displacement through a mass layoff (Displaced_i × event time k)

definition.value: Displaced_i is an indicator equal to one for treated workers who lose their job in a displacement event. A displacement event in year t* requires that (i) the worker separates from their main employer in t* and (ii) employment at the current establishment drops by at least 30 percent in t*. The sample is restricted to workers at most 50 years old in t*−1, with at least three years of tenure with their main employer in t*−1, employed in an establishment with at least 50 employees at the end of t*−1. Workers recalled by their main employer within five years, and events in which more than 20 percent of workers jointly move to another firm, are excluded.

timing.value: Year of the displacement event, t*; the treatment indicator is interacted with event time k = −5, ..., 5 relative to t*

definition.value: The estimated establishment fixed effect ψ̂_{J(i,t)} from the Abowd-Kramarz-Margolis model, equation (2), for log daily wage, where J(i,t) is the main employer of worker i in year t. The AKM model is estimated for each country on the sample of workers with positive earnings, excluding the treated and control workers, with worker and establishment fixed effects, year indicators and a cubic polynomial in age. ψ_{J(i,t)} captures the time-invariant wage policy component for a given employer, denoted the employer-specific wage premium.

timing.value: Measured in calendar year t; the reported coefficient is for event time k = 5, i.e. 5 years after the displacement year t*

units.value: log points of the AKM employer-specific wage premium

magnitude.interpretation: The loss of employer-specific wage premiums is very important in explaining overall wage losses across all countries.

estimand.target_population: Workers in France who are displaced through a mass layoff, satisfy the sample restrictions, are employed, and whose employer belongs to the within-country largest connected set of firms associated with equation (2)

population.description: Workers in France displaced through a mass layoff — at most 50 years old, with at least three years of tenure with their main employer and employed in an establishment with at least 50 employees in the year before displacement — and their 1:1 propensity-score-matched non-displaced control workers
population.ages: at most 50 years old in the year preceding the job displacement event

subgroups_defined: displaced (treated) versus matched control workers

population.selection: Displaced workers are matched 1:1, without replacement, to nearest-neighbour control workers on a propensity score estimated by probit within cells defined by calendar year, gender, and industry; the score uses earnings in t*−2 and t*−3, age, tenure and employer size in t*−1, plus contract type and full-time status where available. Workers recalled by their main employer within five years of displacement are dropped from both groups, and displacement events in which more than 20 percent of workers jointly move to another firm are excluded. Identical sampling restrictions are applied to control workers. For France the data are not the universe of administrative records but a random sample of individuals with all their employment spells (8% of the universe). definition.value: Displaced_i is an indicator equal to one for treated workers who lose their job in a displacement event. A displacement event in year t* requires that (i) the worker separates from their main employer in t* and (ii) employment at the current establishment drops by at least 30 percent in t*. The sample is restricted to workers at most 50 years old in t*−1, with at least three years of tenure with their main employer in t*−1, employed in an establishment with at least 50 employees at the end of t*−1. Workers recalled by their main employer within five years, and events in which more than 20 percent of workers jointly move to another firm, are excluded.

definition.value: The estimated establishment fixed effect ψ̂_{J(i,t)} from the Abowd-Kramarz-Margolis model, equation (2), for log daily wage, where J(i,t) is the main employer of worker i in year t. population.selection: Displaced workers are matched 1:1, without replacement, to nearest-neighbour control workers on a propensity score estimated by probit within cells defined by calendar year, gender, and industry; the score uses earnings in t*−2 and t*−3, age, tenure and employer size in t*−1, plus contract type and full-time status where available. Workers recalled by their main employer within five years of displacement are dropped from both groups, and displacement events in which more than 20 percent of workers jointly move to another firm are excluded. Identical sampling restrictions are applied to control workers. For Italy the data are not the universe of administrative records but a random sample of individuals with all their employment spells (6.5% of the universe). Wages are computed only for the subset of employed workers, and the Table 3 estimates use the subsample of displaced and matched control workers whose employer at time t belongs to the within-country largest connected set of firms associated with equation (2). definition.value: Displaced_i is an indicator equal to one for treated workers who lose their job in a displacement event. population.selection: Displaced workers are matched 1:1, without replacement, to nearest-neighbour control workers on a propensity score estimated by probit within cells defined by calendar year, gender, and industry; the score uses earnings in t*−2 and t*−3, age, tenure and employer size in t*−1, plus contract type and full-time status where available. claims.statement: Job displacement through a mass layoff reduces the employer-specific (AKM) wage premium of displaced workers in Spain by 0.045 log points 5 years after the event, relative to matched non-displaced workers.

treatment.label: Job displacement through a mass layoff (Displaced_i × event time k)

definition.value: Displaced_i is an indicator equal to one for treated workers who lose their job in a displacement event. A displacement event in year t* requires that (i) the worker separates from their main employer in t* and (ii) employment at the current establishment drops by at least 30 percent in t*. The sample is restricted to workers at most 50 years old in t*−1, with at least three years of tenure with their main employer in t*−1, employed in an establishment with at least 50 employees at the end of t*−1. Workers recalled by their main employer within five years, and events in which more than 20 percent of workers jointly move to another firm, are excluded.

timing.value: Year of the displacement event, t*; the treatment indicator is interacted with event time k = −5, ..., 5 relative to t*

definition.value: The estimated establishment fixed effect ψ̂_{J(i,t)} from the Abowd-Kramarz-Margolis model, equation (2), for log daily wage, where J(i,t) is the main employer of worker i in year t. The AKM model is estimated for each country on the sample of workers with positive earnings, excluding the treated and control workers, with worker and establishment fixed effects, year indicators and a cubic polynomial in age. ψ_{J(i,t)} captures the time-invariant wage policy component for a given employer, denoted the employer-specific wage premium.

timing.value: Measured in calendar year t; the reported coefficient is for event time k = 5, i.e. 5 years after the displacement year t*

units.value: log points of the AKM employer-specific wage premium

magnitude.interpretation: The loss of employer-specific wage premiums is very important in explaining overall wage losses across all countries.

population.selection: Displaced workers are matched 1:1, without replacement, to nearest-neighbour control workers on a propensity score estimated by probit within cells defined by calendar year, gender, and industry; the score uses earnings in t*−2 and t*−3, age, tenure and employer size in t*−1, plus contract type and full-time status where available. Workers recalled by their main employer within five years of displacement are dropped from both groups, and displacement events in which more than 20 percent of workers jointly move to another firm are excluded. Identical sampling restrictions are applied to control workers. For Spain the data are not the universe of administrative records but a random sample of individuals with all their employment spells (4% of the universe). Wages are computed only for the subset of employed workers, and the Table 3 estimates use the subsample of displaced and matched control workers whose employer at time t belongs to the within-country largest connected set of firms associated with equation (2). The AKM model, equation (2), is estimated on the country's workers with positive earnings, excluding the treated and control workers.

definition.value: Displaced_i is an indicator equal to one for treated workers who lose their job in a displacement event. A displacement event in year t* requires that (i) the worker separates from their main employer in t* and (ii) employment at the current establishment drops by at least 30 percent in t*. The sample is restricted to workers at most 50 years old in t*−1, with at least three years of tenure with their main employer in t*−1, employed in an establishment with at least 50 employees at the end of t*−1. Workers recalled by their main employer within five years, and events in which more than 20 percent of workers jointly move to another firm, are excluded.

timing.value: Measured in calendar year t; the reported coefficient is for event time k = 5, i.e. 5 years after the displacement year t*

units.value: log points of the daily wage

population.selection: Displaced workers are matched 1:1, without replacement, to nearest-neighbour control workers on a propensity score estimated by probit within cells defined by calendar year, gender, and industry; the score uses earnings in t*−2 and t*−3, age, tenure and employer size in t*−1, plus contract type and full-time status where available. Workers recalled by their main employer within five years of displacement are dropped from both groups, and displacement events in which more than 20 percent of workers jointly move to another firm are excluded. Identical sampling restrictions are applied to control workers. For Spain the data are not the universe of administrative records but a random sample of individuals with all their employment spells (4% of the universe). Wages are computed only for the subset of employed workers, and the Table 3 estimates use the subsample of displaced and matched control workers whose employer at time t belongs to the within-country largest connected set of firms associated with equation (2). claims.statement: Job displacement through a mass layoff reduces the employer-specific (AKM) wage premium of displaced workers in Portugal by 0.044 log points 5 years after the event, relative to matched non-displaced workers.

treatment.label: Job displacement through a mass layoff (Displaced_i × event time k)

register_source.value: Quadros de Pessoal (Portugal); no variable-level register code is named

definition.value: Displaced_i is an indicator equal to one for treated workers who lose their job in a displacement event. A displacement event in year t* requires that (i) the worker separates from their main employer in t* and (ii) employment at the current establishment drops by at least 30 percent in t*. The sample is restricted to workers at most 50 years old in t*−1, with at least three years of tenure with their main employer in t*−1, employed in an establishment with at least 50 employees at the end of t*−1. Workers recalled by their main employer within five years, and events in which more than 20 percent of workers jointly move to another firm, are excluded.

timing.value: Year of the displacement event, t*; the treatment indicator is interacted with event time k = −5, ..., 5 relative to t*

register_source.value: Quadros de Pessoal (Portugal); no variable-level register code is named

definition.value: The estimated establishment fixed effect ψ̂_{J(i,t)} from the Abowd-Kramarz-Margolis model, equation (2), for log daily wage, where J(i,t) is the main employer of worker i in year t. The AKM model is estimated for each country on the sample of workers with positive earnings, excluding the treated and control workers, with worker and establishment fixed effects, year indicators and a cubic polynomial in age. ψ_{J(i,t)} captures the time-invariant wage policy component for a given employer, denoted the employer-specific wage premium.

timing.value: Measured in calendar year t; the reported coefficient is for event time k = 5, i.e. 5 years after the displacement year t*

units.value: log points of the AKM employer-specific wage premium

magnitude.interpretation: The loss of employer-specific wage premiums is very important in explaining overall wage losses across all countries.

population.selection: Displaced workers are matched 1:1, without replacement, to nearest-neighbour control workers on a propensity score estimated by probit within cells defined by calendar year, gender, and industry; the score uses earnings in t*−2 and t*−3, age, tenure and employer size in t*−1, plus contract type and full-time status where available. Workers recalled by their main employer within five years of displacement are dropped from both groups, and displacement events in which more than 20 percent of workers jointly move to another firm are excluded. Identical sampling restrictions are applied to control workers. claims.statement: Job displacement through a mass layoff reduces the log daily wage of displaced workers in Portugal by 0.043 log points 5 years after the event, relative to matched non-displaced workers.

register_source.value: Quadros de Pessoal (Portugal); no variable-level register code is named

definition.value: Displaced_i is an indicator equal to one for treated workers who lose their job in a displacement event. A displacement event in year t* requires that (i) the worker separates from their main employer in t* and (ii) employment at the current establishment drops by at least 30 percent in t*. The sample is restricted to workers at most 50 years old in t*−1, with at least three years of tenure with their main employer in t*−1, employed in an establishment with at least 50 employees at the end of t*−1. Workers recalled by their main employer within five years, and events in which more than 20 percent of workers jointly move to another firm, are excluded.

claims.statement: In Denmark, the loss of employer-specific (AKM) wage premiums accounts for a share 0.44 of the total log daily wage loss suffered by displaced workers 5 years after job displacement.

treatment.label: Job displacement through a mass layoff (Displaced_i × event time k)

definition.value: Displaced_i is an indicator equal to one for treated workers who lose their job in a displacement event. A displacement event in year t* requires that (i) the worker separates from their main employer in t* and (ii) employment at the current establishment drops by at least 30 percent in t*. The sample is restricted to workers at most 50 years old in t*−1, with at least three years of tenure with their main employer in t*−1, employed in an establishment with at least 50 employees at the end of t*−1. Workers recalled by their main employer within five years, and events in which more than 20 percent of workers jointly move to another firm, are excluded.

timing.value: Year of the displacement event, t*; the treatment indicator is interacted with event time k = −5, ..., 5 relative to t*

definition.value: The ratio of the job displacement effect on the employer-specific wage premium (Table 3, column 1) to the overall job displacement effect on log daily wages (Table 3, column 2), at the same event time k. links.pointer_quote: We find that employer-specific wage policies explain a remarkably large share of the observed wage losses for all countries.

claims.statement: In Sweden, the loss of employer-specific (AKM) wage premiums accounts for a share 0.51 of the total log daily wage loss suffered by displaced workers 5 years after job displacement.

treatment.label: Job displacement through a mass layoff (Displaced_i × event time k)

definition.value: Displaced_i is an indicator equal to one for treated workers who lose their job in a displacement event. A displacement event in year t* requires that (i) the worker separates from their main employer in t* and (ii) employment at the current establishment drops by at least 30 percent in t*. The sample is restricted to workers at most 50 years old in t*−1, with at least three years of tenure with their main employer in t*−1, employed in an establishment with at least 50 employees at the end of t*−1. Workers recalled by their main employer within five years, and events in which more than 20 percent of workers jointly move to another firm, are excluded.

timing.value: Year of the displacement event, t*; the treatment indicator is interacted with event time k = −5, ..., 5 relative to t*

outcome.label: Share of the log daily wage loss explained by the loss of employer-specific (AKM) wage premiums

definition.value: The ratio of the job displacement effect on the employer-specific wage premium (Table 3, column 1) to the overall job displacement effect on log daily wages (Table 3, column 2), at the same event time k. The paper describes this as a measure of the share of wage losses explained by changes in employer-specific wage premiums, following Lachowska, Mas, and Woodbury (2020).

timing.value: Event time k = 5, i.e. 5 years after the displacement year t*

units.value: share (ratio of the job loss effect on the employer-specific wage premium to the job loss effect on the log daily wage); 1.00 means the whole wage loss is explained

magnitude.interpretation: Five years after displacement, the change in employer-specific premiums explains between 35 percent and 60 percent of wage losses in Austria, Denmark, Italy, Spain and Sweden; in France this share is almost 70 percent, and in Portugal it reaches 100 percent.

estimand.target_population: Workers in Sweden who are displaced through a mass layoff, are employed, and whose employer belongs to the within-country largest connected set of firms associated with equation (2)

population.selection: Displaced workers are matched 1:1, without replacement, to nearest-neighbour control workers on a propensity score estimated by probit within cells defined by calendar year, gender, and industry; the score uses earnings in t*−2 and t*−3, age, tenure and employer size in t*−1, plus contract type and full-time status where available. Workers recalled by their main employer within five years of displacement are dropped from both groups, and displacement events in which more than 20 percent of workers jointly move to another firm are excluded. Identical sampling restrictions are applied to control workers. Wages are computed only for the subset of employed workers, and the Table 3 estimates use the subsample of displaced and matched control workers whose employer at time t belongs to the within-country largest connected set of firms associated with equation (2).

links.pointer_quote: We find that employer-specific wage policies explain a remarkably large share of the observed wage losses for all countries.

claims.statement: In Austria, the loss of employer-specific (AKM) wage premiums accounts for a share 0.57 of the total log daily wage loss suffered by displaced workers 5 years after job displacement.

treatment.label: Job displacement through a mass layoff (Displaced_i × event time k)

definition.value: Displaced_i is an indicator equal to one for treated workers who lose their job in a displacement event. A displacement event in year t* requires that (i) the worker separates from their main employer in t* and (ii) employment at the current establishment drops by at least 30 percent in t*. The sample is restricted to workers at most 50 years old in t*−1, with at least three years of tenure with their main employer in t*−1, employed in an establishment with at least 50 employees at the end of t*−1. Workers recalled by their main employer within five years, and events in which more than 20 percent of workers jointly move to another firm, are excluded.

timing.value: Year of the displacement event, t*; the treatment indicator is interacted with event time k = −5, ..., 5 relative to t*

outcome.label: Share of the log daily wage loss explained by the loss of employer-specific (AKM) wage premiums

definition.value: The ratio of the job displacement effect on the employer-specific wage premium (Table 3, column 1) to the overall job displacement effect on log daily wages (Table 3, column 2), at the same event time k. timing.value: Event time k = 5, i.e. 5 years after the displacement year t*

units.value: share (ratio of the job loss effect on the employer-specific wage premium to the job loss effect on the log daily wage); 1.00 means the whole wage loss is explained

magnitude.interpretation: Five years after displacement, the change in employer-specific premiums explains between 35 percent and 60 percent of wage losses in Austria, Denmark, Italy, Spain and Sweden; in France this share is almost 70 percent, and in Portugal it reaches 100 percent.

links.pointer_quote: We find that employer-specific wage policies explain a remarkably large share of the observed wage losses for all countries.

claims.statement: In France, the loss of employer-specific (AKM) wage premiums accounts for a share 0.68 of the total log daily wage loss suffered by displaced workers 5 years after job displacement.

treatment.label: Job displacement through a mass layoff (Displaced_i × event time k)

definition.value: Displaced_i is an indicator equal to one for treated workers who lose their job in a displacement event. A displacement event in year t* requires that (i) the worker separates from their main employer in t* and (ii) employment at the current establishment drops by at least 30 percent in t*. The sample is restricted to workers at most 50 years old in t*−1, with at least three years of tenure with their main employer in t*−1, employed in an establishment with at least 50 employees at the end of t*−1. Workers recalled by their main employer within five years, and events in which more than 20 percent of workers jointly move to another firm, are excluded.

timing.value: Year of the displacement event, t*; the treatment indicator is interacted with event time k = −5, ..., 5 relative to t*

outcome.label: Share of the log daily wage loss explained by the loss of employer-specific (AKM) wage premiums

definition.value: The ratio of the job displacement effect on the employer-specific wage premium (Table 3, column 1) to the overall job displacement effect on log daily wages (Table 3, column 2), at the same event time k. The paper describes this as a measure of the share of wage losses explained by changes in employer-specific wage premiums, following Lachowska, Mas, and Woodbury (2020).

timing.value: Event time k = 5, i.e. 5 years after the displacement year t*

units.value: share (ratio of the job loss effect on the employer-specific wage premium to the job loss effect on the log daily wage); 1.00 means the whole wage loss is explained

magnitude.interpretation: Five years after displacement, the change in employer-specific premiums explains between 35 percent and 60 percent of wage losses in Austria, Denmark, Italy, Spain and Sweden; in France this share is almost 70 percent, and in Portugal it reaches 100 percent.

population.selection: Displaced workers are matched 1:1, without replacement, to nearest-neighbour control workers on a propensity score estimated by probit within cells defined by calendar year, gender, and industry; the score uses earnings in t*−2 and t*−3, age, tenure and employer size in t*−1, plus contract type and full-time status where available. Workers recalled by their main employer within five years of displacement are dropped from both groups, and displacement events in which more than 20 percent of workers jointly move to another firm are excluded. Identical sampling restrictions are applied to control workers. For France the data are not the universe of administrative records but a random sample of individuals with all their employment spells (8% of the universe). Wages are computed only for the subset of employed workers, and the Table 3 estimates use the subsample of displaced and matched control workers whose employer at time t belongs to the within-country largest connected set of firms associated with equation (2).

definition.value: Displaced_i is an indicator equal to one for treated workers who lose their job in a displacement event. Workers recalled by their main employer within five years of displacement are dropped from both groups, and displacement events in which more than 20 percent of workers jointly move to another firm are excluded. claims.statement: In Spain, the loss of employer-specific (AKM) wage premiums accounts for a share 0.35 of the total log daily wage loss suffered by displaced workers 5 years after job displacement.

treatment.label: Job displacement through a mass layoff (Displaced_i × event time k)

definition.value: Displaced_i is an indicator equal to one for treated workers who lose their job in a displacement event. A displacement event in year t* requires that (i) the worker separates from their main employer in t* and (ii) employment at the current establishment drops by at least 30 percent in t*. The sample is restricted to workers at most 50 years old in t*−1, with at least three years of tenure with their main employer in t*−1, employed in an establishment with at least 50 employees at the end of t*−1. Workers recalled by their main employer within five years, and events in which more than 20 percent of workers jointly move to another firm, are excluded.

timing.value: Year of the displacement event, t*; the treatment indicator is interacted with event time k = −5, ..., 5 relative to t*

outcome.label: Share of the log daily wage loss explained by the loss of employer-specific (AKM) wage premiums

definition.value: The ratio of the job displacement effect on the employer-specific wage premium (Table 3, column 1) to the overall job displacement effect on log daily wages (Table 3, column 2), at the same event time k. magnitude.interpretation: Five years after displacement, the change in employer-specific premiums explains between 35 percent and 60 percent of wage losses in Austria, Denmark, Italy, Spain and Sweden; in France this share is almost 70 percent, and in Portugal it reaches 100 percent.

population.selection: Displaced workers are matched 1:1, without replacement, to nearest-neighbour control workers on a propensity score estimated by probit within cells defined by calendar year, gender, and industry; the score uses earnings in t*−2 and t*−3, age, tenure and employer size in t*−1, plus contract type and full-time status where available. Workers recalled by their main employer within five years of displacement are dropped from both groups, and displacement events in which more than 20 percent of workers jointly move to another firm are excluded. Identical sampling restrictions are applied to control workers. For Spain the data are not the universe of administrative records but a random sample of individuals with all their employment spells (4% of the universe). Wages are computed only for the subset of employed workers, and the Table 3 estimates use the subsample of displaced and matched control workers whose employer at time t belongs to the within-country largest connected set of firms associated with equation (2).

claims.statement: In Portugal, the loss of employer-specific (AKM) wage premiums accounts for a share 1.01 of the total log daily wage loss suffered by displaced workers 5 years after job displacement.

definition.value: Displaced_i is an indicator equal to one for treated workers who lose their job in a displacement event. A displacement event in year t* requires that (i) the worker separates from their main employer in t* and (ii) employment at the current establishment drops by at least 30 percent in t*. The sample is restricted to workers at most 50 years old in t*−1, with at least three years of tenure with their main employer in t*−1, employed in an establishment with at least 50 employees at the end of t*−1. Workers recalled by their main employer within five years, and events in which more than 20 percent of workers jointly move to another firm, are excluded.

definition.value: The ratio of the job displacement effect on the employer-specific wage premium (Table 3, column 1) to the overall job displacement effect on log daily wages (Table 3, column 2), at the same event time k. population.selection: Displaced workers are matched 1:1, without replacement, to nearest-neighbour control workers on a propensity score estimated by probit within cells defined by calendar year, gender, and industry; the score uses earnings in t*−2 and t*−3, age, tenure and employer size in t*−1, plus contract type and full-time status where available. Workers recalled by their main employer within five years of displacement are dropped from both groups, and displacement events in which more than 20 percent of workers jointly move to another firm are excluded. Identical sampling restrictions are applied to control workers. Wages are computed only for the subset of employed workers, and the Table 3 estimates use the subsample of displaced and matched control workers whose employer at time t belongs to the within-country largest connected set of firms associated with equation (2).

definition.value: A displacement event in year t* = 2010 requires that the worker separates from their main employer in t* and that employment at the current establishment drops by at least 30 percent in t*, with the same sample restrictions as the main analysis (at most 50 years old, at least three years of tenure, establishment with at least 50 employees in t*−1). The 2010 cohort is used to maximize comparability across countries.

timing.value: Displacement year t* = 2010

outcome.label: Share of displaced workers who remain nonemployed

definition.value: The fraction of the 2010 displaced cohort who remain nonemployed, i.e. have not entered the labor market yet, in each of the five years that followed the job displacement event. In panel B the same fraction is computed among those displaced workers who eventually find a job within five years of the displacement event. A person is employed if they have any positive labor earnings during the year.

timing.value: 5 years after the displacement event

units.value: percent of the 2010 displaced cohort

magnitude.interpretation: The figure highlights that between 15 percent and 25 percent of workers in Spain, Italy, and Portugal never reentered the labor market five years postdisplacement.

estimand.target_population: Workers in Spain displaced through a mass layoff in 2010 who satisfy the sample restrictions
estimand.time_horizon: 5 years after the displacement event

population.description: Workers in Spain who suffered a mass-layoff displacement event in the year 2010
population.ages: at most 50 years old in the year preceding the job displacement event
population.period: displacement year 2010, followed for five years
subgroups_defined: all displaced workers (panel A)
displaced workers who eventually find a job within five years (panel B)
population.selection: Conditioned on being displaced in 2010. No control group is used in this figure.

identification.source_of_variation: None: the figure reports raw shares for the 2010 cohort of displaced workers, with no control group and no regression.

key_assumptions.assumption: The 2010 displacement cohort is comparable across countries, which is why it is the cohort chosen for this figure.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as the reason for focusing on the 2010 cohort; footnote 10 states that the results based on the full set of available mass layoff years are qualitatively similar.

key_assumptions.assumption: The figure is conditioned on having been displaced in 2010 (panel A) and, in panel B, additionally on eventually finding a job within five years of displacement.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in the note to Figure 2.

implies_edges.from: displacement in 2010
implies_edges.to: figure sample of displaced workers

threats_discussed: Comparability across countries, which is why the 2010 cohort is used (footnote 10 states that results based on the full set of available mass layoff years are qualitatively similar).
robustness_checks: Footnote 10: the results based on the full set of available mass layoff years are qualitatively similar.
Online Appendix Table A.7 reports the numbers behind each panel.

estimator.value: Descriptive share (no regression): the fraction of the 2010 displaced cohort who remain nonemployed in each year after displacement

source_table.value: Figure 2, Panel A. All displaced workers, Spain, year 5 since displacement

heterogeneity.finding: Only about 20 percent of displaced workers in Sweden, Denmark and France were not able to find a new job in the year right after the displacement event; this fraction is between 30 percent and 40 percent for workers in Italy and Spain and even higher in Portugal, and these differences do not converge over time.
